title: Flow Control
subtitle: Statements, expressions, and the line between them

intro.headline: Some code makes a value. Some code makes things happen.
intro.body:
Aktion is JavaScript, so it inherits JavaScript's oldest split: **expressions** produce a value, **statements** perform an action. In a browser you can ignore the difference for years. Here you cannot — because the right-hand side of every `=` is a value slot, and a UI is built almost entirely out of `=`.

`if`, `switch`, `for`, `while`, `do...while` and `try` are statements. They are fully supported; they simply live in one place — an imperative body. That means a `function`, a lambda written with braces, or an `$effect` callback. Put one on the right of `=` and the parser stops you and names the construct.

That sounds restrictive until you see the replacements. A ternary branches. `.map` loops. A `switch` wrapped in a function and then called does multi-way dispatch. Every one of them is shorter than what it replaces.
intro.codeCaption: the two ways to branch into a value

layers.label: top level
layers.note: bindings, $app, and imperative statements that run once per plan

layers.label: expression position
layers.note: right of an equals sign, a call argument, an array element - values only

layers.label: imperative body
layers.note: function, braced lambda, $effect - the full statement surface

objectives: Name the six block constructs that cannot sit on the right of an `=`
Replace an `if` with a ternary and a `for` with `.map`
Wrap a `switch` in a function so it can produce a value
Break a long line without silently breaking the statement

stages.title: Statements are not values
stages.goal: Tell an expression from a statement before the parser has to.

teach.text:
An **expression** evaluates to something: `2 + 2`, `$rows.length`, `cond ? a : b`, `Card([Text("hi")])`. Anywhere a value is expected — right of `=`, inside a call, inside an array, inside a template hole — only expressions are allowed.

A **statement** performs an action and evaluates to nothing. Six of them show up constantly in UI code: `if`, `switch`, `for` (including `for...of`), `while`, `do...while` and `try`. All six are fully supported — they run inside a `function` body, a lambda written with braces, or an `$effect` callback.

Mix the two up and the parser stops you and names the construct. Write `view = if (…)` and the error reads: `if` is a statement, not an expression — followed by the replacement to use.

code.caption: statements inside the body, an expression on the right of =

parts.text: The whole line is an assignment statement. A program is a list of these.
Everything to the right of this has to be a value. A statement here is a parse error.
A comparison. It evaluates to true or false, so it is welcome on either side.
The only branch that produces a value. Both arms must be expressions too.

tips: `for...of`, `for...in` and the classic three-part `for` are all statements — the loop keyword is what matters, not its shape.

Five of the six get the named diagnostic (`if`, `for`, `switch`, `while`, `try`). `do...while` in expression position falls out as a plain `Unexpected token Keyword "do"` — same rule, blunter message.

tips.text: `let`, `const` and `var` are optional in Aktion and change nothing about this rule. `let x = if (c) {…}` fails exactly the same way.

challenge.title: Only one of these parses
challenge.prompt: Each line tries to pick a view for the current tab. Three of them are parse errors. Which line does the parser accept?

options.detail: The habit from every imperative language. `if` runs a branch; it never hands a value back.

options.code: view = switch ($tab) { case "grid": Grid(cards); default: List(rows) }
options.detail: `switch` is a statement too. It has to be wrapped in a function that returns from each arm.
A loop evaluates to nothing at all. `.map` is the one that returns the array you wanted.

hints: Three of these open with a keyword. The one that parses opens with a value.
Finish the sentence for each line: "the value of this is …". Three of them have no ending.
stages.explain: The parser refuses `if`, `switch` and `for` on the right of `=` for the same reason JavaScript does: they have no value to give you. `if` picks a branch and runs it; `for` runs a body N times; neither one hands anything back to the assignment waiting on the left. A ternary is a different animal — it *is* an expression, so it evaluates to whichever arm it picks, and that value lands in `view`. Because the diagnostic names both the construct and its replacement, this is a mistake you get to make exactly once.

codex.def: An expression evaluates to a value and may sit anywhere a value is expected. A statement performs an action and may only sit in a body — a `function`, a braced lambda, or an `$effect`.

stages.title: The three replacements
stages.goal: Turn each rejected statement into the expression that replaces it.

teach.text:
Every rejected form has a shorter replacement. Learn the three and the restriction stops costing you anything.

A **ternary** replaces `if`. Both arms are expressions, so they can be component calls, and you can chain them (`a ? x : b ? y : z`) when there are three cases.

**`.map`** replaces `for`. It is *the* idiom for turning data into UI — `$rows.map(r => Row([Text(r.title)]))` gives you the array that `Column` and `Grid` already expect. `.filter`, `.reduce` and `.flatMap` are all there too.

For genuine multi-way dispatch, **wrap the `switch` in a function** and `return` from each arm. A function call is an expression, so `view = viewFor($tab)` is perfectly legal — and the `switch` never leaves the body it belongs in. That last move is the general escape hatch: any statement can produce a value if you put it in a function and `return`.

code.src:
banner = $error ? Callout($error, { tone: "danger" }) : Callout("All clear", { tone: "success" })
rows   = $orders.map(o => Text(o.title))
code.caption: ternary for the branch, .map for the loop

code2.caption: the switch stays in a body; the call is the expression

infographic.title: Rejected, and what replaces it
rows: x = for (let r of rows) { Row(r) }
function pick(v) { switch … } then x = pick(v)
return from inside a function body, then call it

tips: Chained ternaries stay readable for two or three cases. Past that, reach for the wrapped `switch`.

tips.text: `.forEach` returns `undefined`. If you want nodes back it has to be `.map`.

challenge.title: Rewrite all three
challenge.prompt: The same three branches, written as expressions. Fill each slot. Three chips in the bank are the statement forms you are replacing — leave those where they are.

hints: The two-character branch is `?` then `:` — condition first, then the true arm, then the false arm.
One array method returns a new array; the other returns nothing. You need the one that returns.
The last slot is the statement you are *allowed* to keep, because it is already inside a function body.
stages.explain: Nothing was lost in the rewrite. The ternary branches, `.map` loops, and the `switch` survives completely untouched — it just moved into a body where statements are legal, and the call `viewFor($tab)` became the expression that carries its result out. Note what makes the third one work: `return`. A `switch` cannot produce a value, but the function around it can, and a call is always an expression.

afterCode.src:
banner = $error ? Callout($error, { tone: "danger" }) : Callout("All clear", { tone: "success" })
rows   = $orders.map(o => Text(o.title))
view   = viewFor($tab)
afterCode.caption: three branches, not one statement on the right

codex.def: A `switch` cannot produce a value, but a function can. Put the switch in a function body, `return` from each arm, and call it: `view = viewFor($tab)`.

preview.program:
$error = null
$orders = [{ title: "AK-1180" }, { title: "AK-1181" }, { title: "AK-1182" }]

$app(Column([
  PageHeader("Orders", { breadcrumbs: false }),
  banner,
  Card([SectionHeader("Open"), Column(rows)])
]))

banner = $error ? Callout($error, { tone: "danger" }) : Callout("All clear", { tone: "success" })

stages.title: Where a line ends
stages.goal: Know which leading token continues a statement — and which one silently starts a new one.

teach.text:
There are no semicolons, so the parser decides where a statement ends by peeking at the next line. If the first significant token there can only *extend* an expression, the line break is swallowed and the statement keeps building.

Those tokens are the operators: `.` `?.` `?` `:` `&&` `||` `??` `==` `!=` `===` `!==` `<` `>` `<=` `>=` `instanceof` `in` `+` `-` `*` `/` `%` `**`, plus the bitwise and shift operators. That is what lets you split a long method chain or a multi-line ternary.

**A `(` or `[` at the start of a line continues nothing.** Same rule as JavaScript's ASI. Break *after* the operator, never before the bracket — otherwise you end up with two statements that both parse, the second one does nothing, and not a single diagnostic fires.

code.caption: a leading . and a leading + keep the statement alive

nodes.label: peek ahead
nodes.note: skip the newlines, find the next real token

nodes.label: an operator?
nodes.note: dot, plus, question mark - swallow the break and keep going

nodes.label: a ( or [ ?
nodes.note: stop - this is a brand new statement

tips.text: `$app` alone on a line with `(Column([...]))` on the next validates cleanly and renders an empty page. It parses as two statements and the root is never called.

challenge.title: One line break too many
challenge.prompt: Four lines here open with a marked token. Three of them continue the statement above. Tap the one that quietly starts a new one — this program validates without a single warning and renders a blank page.
challenge.code:
$cart = [{ label: "Chair", price: 40 }, { label: "Desk", price: 120 }]

total = $util.sum($cart.price)

label = "Subtotal: "
  [[+]] $util.format(total, "currency")

rows = $cart
  [[.filter]](item => item.price > 50)
  [[.map]](item => Text(item.label))

$app
[[(]]Column([rows, Text(label)]))
challenge.fixed:
$cart = [{ label: "Chair", price: 40 }, { label: "Desk", price: 120 }]

total = $util.sum($cart.price)

label = "Subtotal: "
  + $util.format(total, "currency")

rows = $cart
  .filter(item => item.price > 50)
  .map(item => Text(item.label))

$app(Column([rows, Text(label)]))

hints: Three of the four marked tokens are operators. One of them is not.
Ask of each token: could this possibly *extend* the expression on the line above?
Read the last two lines out loud. Is `$app` actually being called at all?
stages.explain: `+`, `.filter` and `.map` are all leading operators, and a leading operator tells the parser to swallow the line break and keep building the same expression — that is exactly how a fluent chain or a wrapped sum is meant to be written. `(` cannot extend anything, so the parser closes `$app` off as a bare expression statement and reads `(Column([...]))` as a second, separate statement. Both parse. Neither renders, because the root was never invoked. This is JavaScript's ASI footgun, inherited whole, and the fix is always the same shape: break *after* an operator, never before a bracket.

afterCode.caption: the call and its parentheses stay on one line

codex.def: A statement continues onto the next line when that line starts with an operator (`.` `?.` `&&` `??` `?` `:` `+` `-` and friends). A leading `(` or `[` starts a new statement instead — so never break a call before its parentheses.

stages.title: The Gate
stages.goal: Route each fragment to the gate that will accept it.

teach.text:
Two gates. The left one is **expression position** — everything to the right of an `=`. The right one is an **imperative body**: a `function`, a braced lambda, an `$effect`.

Steer each falling fragment into the gate that will take it. Statements only fit through `{ body }`. Send one to `= value` and it shatters with the parse error you would have earned.

Eight clean routes clears the stage. Three shattered fragments ends the run.

code.caption: the value gate on the left, the body gate on the right

tips: Move the pointer (or drag) to steer the falling fragment left or right.

tips.text: In real code an expression is welcome inside a body too. The gate that matters is the one that *rejects* — and only `= value` ever rejects anything.

challenge.title: Route the fragments
challenge.prompt: Statements only fit through `{ body }`. Expressions belong at `= value`. Route eight in a row.
challenge.note: Move the pointer to steer the falling fragment. A statement sent to the value gate shatters.
challenge.winNote: Press Check to bank the XP.

fallback.prompt: The value gate accepts exactly one of these. Which fragment is legal on the right-hand side of `=`?

options.detail: `if` runs a branch. It has no value to assign.
A loop produces nothing. `.map` produces the array.
Legal inside a function body, never on the right of an equals sign.

hints: Anything that opens with a keyword — `if`, `for`, `switch`, `while`, `do`, `try` — is a statement.
Anything with `?` and `:`, `.map`, `??`, or a bare call is an expression.
If it can finish the sentence "the value of this is …", steer it left.
stages.explain: The gate is not a metaphor for style — it is literally what the parser does. When it reads `x =` it switches into expression mode, and the only thing it will accept there is something that can produce a value. A keyword like `for` in that position has nowhere to go, so the parse stops and names the construct. Inside a body the parser is in statement mode, where expressions and statements are both welcome. That asymmetry is why every replacement in this world works the same way: move the statement into a body, and carry its result out through a `return`.

codex.def: Any slot where the parser expects a value: right of `=`, a call argument, an array element, a ternary arm, a template hole. Statements are rejected there and nowhere else.

stages.title: What the operators actually return
stages.goal: Predict the result of ==, === and < before you run them.

teach.text:
Comparison in Aktion is JavaScript's, coercion and all, because the runtime hands the operands to the engine.

`==` and `!=` are **abstract**: `1 == "1"` is `true`, `0 == false` is `true`, and the one you actually want — `x == null` — is `true` for both `null` and `undefined`. `===` and `!==` stay strict. Use `== null` deliberately as a two-in-one guard, and `===` everywhere else.

Relational `<` and `>` compare alphabetic strings lexicographically, so `arr.sort((a, b) => a.name > b.name ? 1 : -1)` orders correctly. `Date` operands coerce through `valueOf`, so `new Date(a) > new Date(b)` compares the instants rather than silently comparing two zeroes.

One documented divergence to keep in your head: **two numeric strings compare numerically**, so `"5" < "10"` is `true` in Aktion and `false` in plain JavaScript. Convenient when API data arrives as strings — surprising if you assume pure JS.

code.src:
guard  = $draft == null ? "nothing saved" : "draft ready"
byName = $people.sort((a, b) => a.name > b.name ? 1 : -1)
newest = new Date($a.created) > new Date($b.created)
code.caption: one abstract guard, one lexicographic sort, one date compare

infographic.title: Two guards that are not the same

columns.title: Catches both
columns.note: true for null AND undefined - the guard you almost always want

columns.title: Catches one
columns.note: misses undefined, and an atom that was never assigned is undefined, not null

tips: `x == null` is the single place `==` beats `===`. Reach for it on purpose, not by accident.

tips.text: Relational `<` and `>` are the one corner where Aktion deviates from JavaScript: two numeric strings compare by value.

challenge.title: Which rule fires first
challenge.prompt: Relational `<` does one thing to both operands, then tries three rules and stops at the first that fits. Tap all four in the order Aktion runs them — the order that makes `"5" < "10"` come out `true`.
challenge.help: One chip is the preparation step every comparison starts with. The other three are the rules, and the first rule that fits decides the result.
challenge.code:
sortsRight = "beta" < "gamma"
byInstant  = new Date($a.created) > new Date($b.created)
mixedPair  = $rows.length < "10"
apiStrings = "5" < "10"
order: two numeric strings? compare by value
two strings? compare letter by letter

hints: Nothing can be tested until both sides are primitives — that is what makes `new Date(a) > new Date(b)` compare instants instead of two zeroes.
If the letter-by-letter rule ran first, `"5" < "10"` would be `false`, because `"5"` outranks `"1"`. It is `true`, so something has to run ahead of it.
One rule asks nothing at all — it just takes whatever the others did not claim. That can only be last.
stages.explain: `==` runs JavaScript's abstract-equality algorithm, which makes it exactly right once: `x == null` as a combined null-and-undefined guard. Everywhere else `===` saves you an argument in review. Relational `<` is the interesting one — each operand is coerced with the number hint first (that is what makes `Date` work), alphabetic strings then fall through to lexicographic order (that is what makes comparator sorts work), and one deliberate convenience survives on top: two numeric strings compare by value. Real JavaScript would tell you `"5" < "10"` is false. Aktion says true. Worth remembering the next time you sort an API payload that arrived as strings.

codex.def: Abstract equality against `null` is `true` for both `null` and `undefined` — the one place `==` beats `===`. Use it as a single guard for "no value yet"; use `===` everywhere else.

preview.program:
$draft = null

$app(Column([
  PageHeader("Draft", { breadcrumbs: false }),
  $draft == null
    ? Callout("Nothing saved yet", { tone: "info", description: "== null catches null and undefined in one guard." })
    : Card([Text($draft)])
]))

stages.title: Dispatch on a tab
stages.goal: Write a multi-way dispatch with no statement on the right of an equals sign.

teach.text:
Everything from this world comes together in one small program.

`$tab` holds the current view. A `switch` decides which component to build — so it goes inside a function that `return`s from every arm, and the call becomes the expression. The grid arm builds its children with `.map`, because a `for` loop cannot hand you an array.

Two shortcuts are worth using while you are here. `$rows.length` works on any array. And reading a plain property off an array **plucks** it: `$rows.title` gives you `["Invoice", "Receipt"]` — exactly the shape `List` and `Col` want, with no lambda at all. `.first` and `.last` sit on the same path.

code.caption: the shape, not the answer — you still have to build cards and labels

tips: Every arm needs its own `return`. An arm that falls through gives the caller `undefined` and renders nothing.
`default:` is the arm that keeps the page alive when `$tab` holds something you did not plan for.

challenge.title: Write the dispatch
challenge.prompt: `$tab` and `$rows` are declared for you. Write `function viewFor(tab)` whose `switch` returns a `Grid` of `Card`s for `"grid"` — built with `.map` — and a `List` for everything else. Then render `viewFor($tab)` from a single `$app(...)`.

mustWhy: Wrap the switch in a function called viewFor — that is what lets it produce a value.
The dispatch itself is a switch. It is legal here because it sits inside a body.
Each arm has to return its component; an arm that falls through renders nothing.
Build the grid children with .map — a for loop cannot hand you an array.
Call viewFor($tab). The call is the expression that goes into the tree.

hints: Start with `function viewFor(tab) {`, then `switch (tab) {` inside it.
Every `case` needs its own `return`, and `default:` catches the rest.
`Grid($rows.map(r => Card([Text(r.title)])), { columns: 3 })` is the grid arm; `List($rows.title)` is the list arm.
stages.explain: Look at where the `switch` ended up: inside a body, exactly where statements are allowed, with its value escaping through `return`. `viewFor($tab)` is then an ordinary call — an expression — so it drops straight into the tree next to `PageHeader`. That single move covers every statement you will ever want a value out of. And `List($rows.title)` is the array-pluck shortcut doing the work of `.map(r => r.title)`: reading a plain property off an array maps it across the items, which is why column-oriented components like `Col` and `List` read so cleanly.

afterCode.caption: a statement, safely producing a value

codex.def: Reading a non-array property off an array maps it across the items: `$rows.title` is `["Invoice", "Receipt"]`. `.length`, `.first` and `.last` are shortcuts on the same path.

preview.caption: live — a switch producing a value, rendered by the real runtime

outro.headline: The line between them is visible now
outro.body: Expressions go anywhere. Statements go in a body. Every construct the parser rejects on the right of `=` has a shorter replacement — a ternary, a `.map`, or a function that wraps the statement and returns from it. And when a program parses but renders nothing, check where your line breaks fell before you check anything else.
outro.nextHint: Next up: reactive data — `$http` and its relatives hand back a bag rather than a payload, and every branch you just learned goes to work on `.loading`, `.error` and `.data`.
